articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License, Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This action modifies existing authorizations pertaining to transactions involving Venezuela.

The specifics of the amendments to the General License and the content of the new FAQ were not immediately detailed in the announcement. However, such updates typically aim to clarify the scope of permissible activities under the Venezuela sanctions program or adjust existing restrictions in response to ongoing developments.

Entities and individuals engaging in Venezuela-related transactions are advised to review the updated guidance carefully to ensure compliance with the evolving sanctions landscape. OFAC regularly updates its sanctions programs through new designations, program modifications, and general license issuances.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Sanctions on Iran and Cuba, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran and a designation concerning Cuba on October 15, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to accompany these actions.

While specific details of the designated entities and individuals were not immediately public, the announcement indicated that the new sanctions and licensing actions are aimed at Iran and Cuba. Previous reports from Africanews on October 16, 2026, indicated that OFAC had targeted 16 individuals and 11 entities in Iran, including financial institutions, currency exchange firms, and energy and trading companies. Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) was also reportedly designated due to its ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank.

The inclusion of Iran and Cuba in new sanctions raises questions about potential additional constraints on energy and commodity exports or on shipping, insurance, and financial channels that enable those exports. Markets are expected to price in higher geopolitical and policy risk premiums until the full scope of the measures is clarified.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a de-listing of an individual or entity previously subject to U.S. sanctions targeting the Venezuelan government or individuals associated with it.

Designation removals by OFAC can occur for various reasons, including a change in circumstances, a determination that the criteria for designation are no longer met, or as part of broader diplomatic or policy shifts. Such removals can ease restrictions on the delisted party and those who wish to engage in transactions with them.

The specific identity of the removed party was not immediately disclosed in the brief announcement. However, this action reflects the dynamic nature of sanctions programs and OFAC's ongoing review of designated individuals and entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities on October 13, 2026. This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting illicit financial networks that support drug trafficking and terrorist organizations.

These designations aim to isolate the targeted parties from the international financial system, blocking their assets and generally prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them. Such measures are critical tools in combating global illicit finance and protecting national security.

While the specific names of the designated individuals and entities were not immediately available, these actions are part of ongoing efforts to combat transnational criminal organizations and those who commit or support terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, International Criminal Court Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations by the logistics company.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also announced a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC), along with the issuance of new General Licenses (GLs). Additionally, a Burma-related designation was removed.

The details of the settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, including the nature of the violations, were not immediately specified in the announcement. However, the settlement amount was later revealed to be $175,015. The ICC designation and the Burma-related removal reflect the dynamic and multifaceted nature of OFAC's enforcement and sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026. This action provides authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are crucial tools used by OFAC to carve out specific permissible activities from broader sanctions, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain types of trade, or other policy objectives. The issuance of a new GL suggests an adjustment to the scope of existing restrictions on Russia.

The specifics of what the new General License authorizes were not immediately detailed in the announcement. However, entities engaging in Russia-related transactions should review the new guidance to understand any newly permitted activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued an Iran-related General License (GL) and an amended Russia-related General License.

The Iran-related designations target individuals or entities deemed to be involved in activities contrary to U.S. foreign policy objectives concerning Iran. The accompanying Iran-related GL likely provides specific authorizations to mitigate unintended consequences or facilitate certain transactions.

The amendment to the Russia-related General License indicates a modification to existing authorizations for transactions involving Russia. These actions reflect the ongoing and evolving nature of U.S. sanctions policy towards both Iran and Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Alert, Updates FAQs, and Removes Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several actions related to Iran on October 5, 2026, including designations removals, designations updates, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert. Additionally, an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) was published.

The designations removals and updates indicate adjustments to the list of individuals and entities subject to Iran sanctions, potentially reflecting changes in their activities or ownership. The OFAC Alert likely provides guidance or warnings regarding specific risks or evasion tactics related to Iran sanctions.

The amended FAQ offers clarification on existing regulations, helping individuals and entities better understand their compliance obligations. These actions collectively demonstrate OFAC's continuous efforts to refine and enforce its Iran sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting or engaging in terrorism.

These actions are part of the U.S. government's broader strategy to combat global terrorism by disrupting financial flows and networks that enable terrorist activities. Designated parties have their assets blocked and are generally prohibited from engaging in transactions with U.S. persons.

The specific details of the designated individuals and entities were not immediately released. However, such designations serve as a critical tool in isolating terrorist financiers and facilitators from the international financial system.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Department of the Treasury against the bank for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

Bank of America agreed to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. These violations occurred due to issues such as channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, allowing designated individuals to transact due to poor sanctions alert calibration, and failing to promptly update watchlists.

The OFAC penalty, alongside a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC, underscores the critical importance of robust compliance programs for financial institutions to mitigate illicit finance risks.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This penalty marks the largest in OCC history.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with its transaction monitoring system failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This led to the filing of numerous late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many of which indicated money laundering.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance and did not complete significant steps needed to establish an effective program. The OCC emphasized that such egregious and continued BSA violations warrant swift and significant action.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express for AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank and its parent and affiliated entities on October 8, 2026. This action addresses significant deficiencies in the institution's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs, along with enterprise-wide financial crimes compliance programs.

The OCC found that American Express's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training. Specifically, the bank's risk assessment did not sufficiently address the risks associated with its credit and charge-card business, and there were systemic breakdowns in suspicious-activity monitoring, investigation, and reporting.

These deficiencies contributed to the bank's processing of approximately $13 billion in suspected trade-based money laundering activity from June 2014 through May 2025. The OCC emphasized that institutions must ensure their risk assessments accurately reflect their businesses and that boards and senior management are positioned to oversee remediation of significant deficiencies.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

body: Polling suggests most Albertans favour remaining part of the country, although the debate alone has proven divisive.

articles.headline: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
body: Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie faces 191 murder charges - all but one of them children.

articles.headline: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
body: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.

articles.headline: Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote
body: The race heats up just days before the run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing challenger.

articles.headline: Italian PM Meloni to hold emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
body: More than 200 people were detained during two days of rioting in the city, Italian media reports.

articles.headline: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
body: Saudi Arabia said it executed two Bangladeshis last week for committing an "indecent act" in a mosque.

articles.headline: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
body: Researchers travelled to a remote Pacific Island to confirm whether an object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the mystery of the pilot's disappearance.

articles.headline: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
body: The blaze that killed four men and injured dozens of others spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest.

articles.headline: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting attempt in Mumbai
body: Videos showed gunmen firing shots at Shroff's car while it was moving slowly past a crowd.

articles.headline: Bomb threat forces Israel to Austria flight into emergency landing
body: The Airbus jet landed safely in Bulgaria and all passengers and crew aboard were unharmed, officials said.

articles.headline: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
body: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.

articles.headline: Musk and Anthropic pledge public share giveaways
body: Musk's announcement comes after Anthropic pledged to create a public benefit fund ahead of its blockbuster stock market listing.

articles.headline: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
body: Jordon Steele-John says the timing of the claims is motivated by "nasty political games" within the Greens.

articles.headline: Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
body: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.

articles.headline: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
body: BBC News hears from users, dealers, prison and recovery workers as the country battles with a deadly new drug epidemic.

articles.headline: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
body: An international rescue operation for the last 30 captive whales in Canada made headlines. Then five of them died.

articles.headline: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
body: The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from Chicago, where communities are battling a new wave of synthetic drugs.

articles.headline: Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery
body: The Pope's first event since his lung cancer diagnosis and surgery saw him recite the traditional Angelus prayer from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.

articles.headline: Watch: Shops looted and restaurants gutted in Paris riots
body: Violence broke out across France, with more than half a million people taking to the streets over the weekend.

articles.headline: How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France
body: Demonstrations across the country turned violent, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked.
